Grisons
gree-ZOHN
n. (the Three Leagues of the eastern Alps, German Graubünden, reformed by the Ilanz articles and the first land to have Scripture in Romansh)
French Grisons, from the Grey League, German Graubunden, the grey leagues, for the undyed homespun of its peasants; Romansh Grischun.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Grisons were a federation of three leagues of Alpine valleys, allied to the Swiss but not a canton, governed by the votes of its communes, and that constitution shaped its Reformation. The Articles of Ilanz, agreed by the leagues in 1524 and extended in 1526, did not establish a religion; they subjected the clergy to civil courts, forbade appeals to foreign bishops, required that preaching be from Scripture, and then left each commune free to choose its own faith by its own vote. The result was a permanently mixed country, parish by parish, with Reformed and Catholic valleys side by side. Johannes Comander at Chur and Philipp Gallicius organised the Reformed side, the synod of Chur governed it, and the leagues' Romansh-speaking communes received Scripture in their own tongue, Jachiam Bifrun printing the New Testament in Ladin in 1560. The leagues also ruled the Italian-speaking Valtellina as subject territory, where in July 1620 the Catholic party massacred several hundred Protestants in what is called the Sacro Macello, and the Thirty Years War then came through the passes. The dictionary enters the Grisons because a commune-by-commune vote is the nearest thing in the Reformation to a settlement by consent, and it produced neither uniformity nor peace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a league as a confederacy; a commune as a small territorial district; a pass as a narrow passage through mountains; and a massacre as the murder of many with cruelty.

expand to see more

LEAGUE, n. An alliance or confederacy between princes or states for their mutual aid or defense.

COMMUNE, n. A small territorial district in some European countries, with its own local government.

PASS, n. A narrow passage, entrance or avenue; a narrow or difficult place of entrance and exit, as a defile.

MASSACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers, with cruelty or atrocity.

SYNOD, n. A council or meeting of ecclesiastics to consult on matters of religion.

Key Scripture

Act 2:11 — "Cretes and Arabians, we do hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God."

Psa 104:18 — "The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies."

Rev 6:9 — "And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:"

Isa 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Modern Corruption

Three Leagues of the eastern Alps whose Ilanz articles of 1524 left each commune to choose its faith, and where the Valtellina massacre of 1620 killed several hundred Protestants.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the massacre done for religion, and the Grisons carry one of the worst in the Alps. In July 1620 the Catholic party of the Valtellina, the leagues' Italian-speaking subject valley, killed several hundred of their Protestant neighbours over some days; the dictionary names it plainly and also names the provocation, which was years of Grisons rule imposed by a foreign-speaking Protestant federation on a Catholic population it governed as subjects rather than as members. Neither fact excuses the other. The company under the altar is drawn from both sides of many such quarrels, those “slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) being counted by God and not by us.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that preaching from the text, which Ilanz required of every minister in the leagues, is a better foundation than a uniform settlement imposed from a capital. “To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) was written into the articles themselves. The leagues also did the translator's work for a tongue almost nobody spoke, so that Romansh shepherds in the high valleys could “hear them speak in our tongues the wonderful works of God” (Act 2:11), among rocks where “The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats” (Psa 104:18).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew torah (H8451), law, instruction; Greek glossa (G1100), a tongue; Hebrew machseh (H4268), a refuge.

expand to see more

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction, that which is taught; “To the law and to the testimony”, Isaiah 8:20.

Greek glossa (G1100) — a tongue, and so a language; “hear them speak in our tongues”, Acts 2:11.

Hebrew machseh (H4268) — a shelter, a refuge; “The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats”, Psalm 104:18.

Greek sphazo (G4969) — to slay, to kill by violence; “them that were slain for the word of God”, Revelation 6:9.

Greek marturia (G3141) — a testimony borne; “the testimony which they held”, Revelation 6:9.

Usage

"“To the law and to the testimony” (Isa 8:20) — the Ilanz articles requiring preaching from Scripture, 1524."

"“hear them speak in our tongues” (Act 2:11) — Bifrun's Romansh New Testament of 1560."

"“them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) — the Valtellina massacre of July 1620."
